A sky-diver falls vertically from a helicopter and reaches constant (terminal) velocity. The graph
shows the variation with time t of the speed v of the sky-diver.

hints: Notice the $v$-$t$ graph starts at $v=0$ at $t=0$, rises steeply, then flattens to horizontal at terminal velocity.
Recall that the gradient of a $d$-$t$ graph equals speed, so $d$-$t$ gradient must start at zero and then grow as $v$ grows.
Check what constant $v$ at large $t$ means for $d$: distance must keep increasing at a steady rate, so the $d$-$t$ graph must end as a straight line with positive gradient.
walkthrough: The given $v$-$t$ graph starts at the origin, so initial speed is zero, then $v$ increases and finally stays constant at terminal velocity.
For distance fallen, $v = \frac{\Delta d}{\Delta t}$, so the gradient of the $d$-$t$ graph at any time equals the instantaneous speed $v$ at that time.
At $t=0$, $v=0$, so the $d$-$t$ graph must start with zero gradient, flat at the origin, then get steeper while the sky-diver accelerates.
Later $v$ becomes constant, so the $d$-$t$ gradient must become constant, meaning the $d$-$t$ graph becomes a straight line with positive slope and $d$ continues to increase.
Only the curve that is flat at the origin, curves upward, then continues upward as a straight line matches this, and This is option C

A.explanation: Gradient increases without limit to a steep straight line, which would mean speed keeps increasing rather than levelling at terminal velocity.

B.explanation: Distance levels off to zero gradient, which would mean the sky-diver stops falling, contradicting continued fall at terminal velocity.

C.explanation: Gradient starts at zero, increases as speed increases, then becomes constant and positive when terminal velocity is reached.

D.explanation: Gradient starts steep and decreases, which would mean high initial speed that slows down, opposite to starting from rest and speeding up.
